newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. presses Bosnians to create government.
newsitem.headline: U.S. presses Bosnians to create government.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher pressed Bosnia's three-man presidency on Wednesday to name a cabinet and bring to life the government of their ethnically divided state.

Christopher also condemned what his spokesman called a "very disappointing" incident in which Bosnian Serbs clashed with Moslems on Tuesday and called on the rival factions to respect freedom of movement enshrined in the Dayton peace pact.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns made clear that Washington held the Serbs primarily to blame for the incident in which Bosnian Serbs fired on Moslem refugees seeking to return to their homes in what is now Serb territory.
The hour-long meeting took place the day before an international conference in Paris is due to adopt a two-year plan to consolidate peace in the former Yugoslav republic.

Despite elections in September, continuing tension between the Moslems, Serbs and Croats has hindered creation of a functioning government for the two-part Bosnian state foreseen by the Dayton accord, signed a year ago.
Burns said Christopher told the three leaders that "the focus of their efforts had to be in positioning (the Bosnian) state to provide stability and continuing peace for the citizens of that state".

"That means the creation of a council of ministers, the creation of the other unified institutions -- the parliamentary assembly, the central bank, the judicial system including a high court," Burns told reporters.
Christopher met at his Paris hotel with Moslem Alija Izetbegovic, Serb Momcilo Krajisnik and Croat Kresimir Zubak.
It was the first time the three co-presidents have appeared together on the international stage. But their collegiality does not yet stretch to sharing an aircraft.
Western officials said Krajisnik refused to fly to Paris in the same plane as the two others and travelled instead from Belgrade, capital of rump Yugoslavia.
After Christopher left the meeting, Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum held further meetings with the Bosnian leaders to try to get them to agree a cabinet list as soon as possible.
Ethnic rivalries have so far prevented the co-presidents from naming a government despite a previous commitment to do so by November 1.

Burns said Christopher listed freedom of movement between Bosnia's two entities as a priority issue and raised "the very disappointing event of yesterday and today in which Moslem citizens were fired upon for seeking to return to their homes".

Burns said that although Moslems had failed to complete formalities for seeking to return to their homes, "there can be no excuse for the actions of the Bosnian Serbs in firing on these people and seeking to intimidate them".
"Secretary Christopher was clearly calling upon the Bosnian Serbs to show restraint," he added.
Krajisnik acknowledged the importance of the refugee issue -- some two million people have been displaced in Bosnia -- but made no immediate response to the U.S. criticisms, Burns said.

Other issues raised by Christopher included the need to hand over accused war criminals, the importance of future municipal elections in Bosnia, and the importance of respecting arms control agreements.

Burns said Christopher again pressed Izetbegovic to fire his deputy defence minister, Hasan Cengic, who Washington says is obstructing a U.S. plan to equip and train the forces of Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation.
The United States is witholding delivery of $100 million of arms until Cengic is dismissed. Izetbegovic has several times promised to comply, but Cengic is still at his post.
"I would expect this issue will be taken care of," Burns said without elaborating.
The co-presidents earlier had lunch with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and told reporters they had agreed Thursday's conference should give a boost to slow-moving civilian reconstruction.
